desc:
A sorted array of distinct integers was cut at some position into a front part and a back part and the two parts were swapped, producing nums. For example [11, 15, 6, 8, 9, 10] comes from [6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 15].

Return the number of index pairs (i, j) with i < j and nums[i] + nums[j] == target. For the array above and target = 19 the answer is 2 (8 + 11 and 9 + 10). Do not sort or copy the array; O(n) time with O(1) extra space is expected.
constraints: nums is a rotation of a sorted array
hints: For a sorted array the two-pointer technique counts the pairs in linear time. What changes when the array is rotated?
Find the index s of the smallest element. Starting from there and walking circularly gives the sorted order.

Run two pointers over virtual positions 0..n-1, reading each value as nums[(s + pos) % n]: if the sum is too small advance the left pointer, if too large retreat the right pointer, and count a hit by moving both.
editorial: The pair sum does not depend on the order of the array, so we can pretend to work on the sorted version. A virtual array v[j] = nums[(s + j) % n] is sorted when s is the index of the minimum, and it costs nothing to build because we only translate indices.

Find s with the binary search that compares nums[mid] to nums[hi] (O(log n)). Then keep left = 0 and right = n - 1. While left < right: if v[left] + v[right] < target move left up; if it is larger move right down; if equal count one pair and move both. Because values are distinct, each value takes part in at most one matching pair, so moving both pointers loses nothing. Time O(n), space O(1).
